description: Width tiers for Year 9 Science — ACARA v9. Covers the seven U-strand descriptors. H-strand and I-strand (9–10 band) are in science_y9_10_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term — the fewest phenomena or contexts that still genuinely satisfy what the descriptor requires.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor grounded in the most common elaboration cases.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding phenomena, cultural contexts or applications. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data. Typical grounded in common cases; wider may infer within the descriptor's territory and year band.

AC9S9U01.minimum_width: Trace the receptor-command centre-effector pathway for one named stimulus; distinguish nervous from endocrine system roles; describe negative feedback for one homeostatic mechanism identifying set point, deviation, corrective response and return detection.
AC9S9U01.typical_width: Compare nervous (electrical, fast) and endocrine (chemical, slower) coordination across multiple stimuli; trace receptor-command-effector pathways for temperature, blood glucose and exercise; describe negative feedback for multiple homeostatic systems; model pathways using flow diagrams; explain the effect of a feedback disorder.
wider: Analyse how imaging technologies (MRI, CT, PET) have improved understanding of body system interactions — connecting technology advance to scientific knowledge (AC9S9H02)
Investigate how understanding of feedback mechanisms enabled development of pharmaceuticals (insulin, electrolytes in sports drinks)
Examine how a feedback system disorder (diabetes, hypothyroidism) disrupts the receptor-command-effector pathway at a specific point
elaborations: exploring the body's observable responses to external stimuli (such as changes in light or temperature, or presence of danger or pathogens) or internal stimuli (such as dehydration or hunger)
using models, flow diagrams and virtual simulations to explore and represent the relationships between body systems that are necessary to coordinate a response to stimuli
comparing the role and function of electrical impulses and hormones in the body's responses to external stimuli
modelling how the process of regulation is monitored and adjusted by connections between the receptor, command centre and effector
examining the effects of a disorder in a feedback system, such as diabetes-induced blindness or hypothermia

considering how understanding of feedback mechanisms has enabled the development of pharmaceuticals and other products to address issues or enhance performance, such as insulin or electrolytes in sports drinks

AC9S9U02.minimum_width: Describe at least two structural features of each gamete type and explain how each relates to function; explain that sexual reproduction produces greater variation than asexual; give one reason why variation is important for survival.
AC9S9U02.typical_width: Explain how gamete form reflects function; describe how reproductive organs work as a system; explain fertilisation as genetic combination; compare sexual and asexual reproduction in terms of variation produced; explain how variation supports adaptability; examine reproductive strategies across organisms including parental care trade-offs.
wider: Compare gamete structure across animal groups — internal vs external fertilisers — and explain how structure relates to fertilisation strategy
Examine how the number of offspring relates to parental care — analysing the survival trade-off between many offspring with low care vs few with high care
Research how assisted reproductive technologies have become widely used since initial development — examining the adoption factors (AC9S9H03)
elaborations: examining how the male and female reproductive organ structures work collectively as a system
explaining how the forms of male and female gametes relate to their specific function
identifying and comparing sexual and asexual reproductive strategies in plants
exploring how sexual reproduction creates a greater rate of variation among offspring compared with asexual reproduction
examining how the reproductive strategies of multicellular animals are related to their environment and the complexity of the organism
examining how the number of offspring produced by animals is related to the amount of parental care

AC9S9U03.minimum_width: Name and describe Earth's four spheres with one interaction example; explain how photosynthesis, respiration and combustion each move carbon between named spheres; represent the carbon cycle in a diagram; describe the greenhouse effect.
AC9S9U03.typical_width: Describe sphere interactions across multiple examples; represent the complete carbon cycle with processes and stores; explain human combustion impact on atmospheric CO₂; describe the greenhouse effect and amplification; identify carbon sequestration strategies; connect to scientific consensus on global warming.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional fire regimes affect carbon cycling differently from European-style fire management — examining the emissions implications
Calculate a carbon footprint and identify which human activities contribute most to atmospheric CO₂
Examine carbon capture and storage technologies as human interventions in the cycle — evaluating effectiveness and limitations
Conduct a field investigation to estimate carbon sequestration in a local ecosystem using tree biomass and soil measurements
elaborations: identifying Earth as a system, describing Earth's spheres and discussing examples of interactions between different spheres
examining the carbon cycle using diagrams, animations or simulations and explaining the role of photosynthesis and respiration in that cycle
identifying the impact of combustion reactions as a result of human activity on the carbon cycle
investigating the greenhouse effect and relating it to the role carbon dioxide plays in maintaining temperatures that support life on Earth
conducting a field investigation to evaluate carbon sequestration in an ecosystem
investigating how First Nations Australians use fire-mediated chemical reactions to facilitate energy and nutrient transfer through firestick farming
investigating how First Nations Australians are reducing greenhouse gas emissions through traditional fire management
identifying how carbon dioxide is captured and stored naturally or through technologies
calculating an individual's carbon footprint and suggesting strategies to reduce emissions

AC9S9U04.minimum_width: Explain conduction and convection using the particle model; explain electrical current as directed particle movement; explain sound as a wave requiring a medium and EM radiation as a wave that can travel through a vacuum; identify one phenomenon better explained by each model.
AC9S9U04.typical_width: Explain conduction, convection and electrical conductors/insulators using particle model; model sound transfer with wave representations; describe EM spectrum regions and their uses; explain why EM radiation travels through vacuum but sound does not; evaluate wave vs particle model usefulness for different phenomena including wave-particle duality of light.
wider: Investigate heat transfer and conservation in First Nations Australians' bedding and clothing across different climatic regions
Investigate the impact of material selection on sound energy transfer in First Nations Australians' traditional musical, hunting and communication instruments
Examine how properties of EM radiation relate to specific uses: radar, medicine, mobile communications, remote sensing, microwave cooking (AC9S9H02)
Discuss wave-particle duality of light including the photon concept — examining how two models can both be useful without either being complete
elaborations: describing the processes underlying convection and conduction of heat in terms of the particle model
modelling the transfer of sound energy as waves using slinky springs and relating to the medium through which the sound is transferred
examining how the particle model of electricity explains static electricity and electrical current and relating this to voltage, conductors and insulators
discussing the wave and particle models of energy transfer, including the concept of photons, and how they are useful for understanding aspects of light and other forms of electromagnetic radiation
investigating aspects of heat transfer and conservation in the design of First Nations Australians' bedding and clothing in the various climatic regions of Australia
investigating the impact of material selection on the transfer of sound energy in First Nations Australians' traditional musical, hunting and communication instruments
examining the forms of electromagnetic radiation that are used in different modern communication technologies and identifying any limitations

AC9S9U05.minimum_width: State the law of conservation of energy; explain that all energy outputs (useful + wasted) sum to total input; calculate efficiency using useful output ÷ total input; draw or interpret a Sankey diagram.
AC9S9U05.typical_width: Apply conservation of energy to explain why wasted heat does not mean energy destruction; calculate efficiency for multiple systems; construct and critique Sankey diagrams with correct ratios; compare electricity generation efficiency from different sources; interpret energy star ratings; explain why 100% efficiency is unachievable.
wider: Investigate the efficiency of ground ovens used by First Nations Australians — comparing with modern cooking methods
Compare efficiency of electricity generation from coal, solar, wind, nuclear and hydro — examining trade-offs (AC9S9H04)
Examine energy star rating criteria for appliances and evaluate how efficiency improvements reduce running costs and emissions
Investigate how improving efficiency in pole vaulting or archery applies conservation of energy to optimise athletic performance
elaborations: explaining that the law of conservation of energy explains that total energy is maintained in energy transfer and transformation in a system
explaining efficiency and recognising that in energy transfer and transformation a variety of processes can occur, so that the amount of usable energy is reduced and the system is not 100% efficient
using and critiquing representations such as Sankey diagrams to show energy inputs, changes and outputs in a system
investigating the efficiency of ground ovens used by First Nations Australians
comparing the efficiency of electricity generation from coal and other sources such as nuclear, hydroelectricity, gas, solar and wind
examining the meaning of energy star ratings given to appliances such as refrigerators and washing machines and criteria used to determine these ratings
examining how improving efficiency in energy transfer and transformations in sporting activities such as pole vaulting or archery improves athletic performance

AC9S9U06.minimum_width: Describe at least two atomic model revisions with the evidence that prompted each; explain what an isotope is; describe at least two types of radioactive decay with examples; define half-life and use it to calculate remaining mass.
AC9S9U06.typical_width: Trace atomic model development from Dalton through Thomson, Rutherford to Bohr with evidence for each revision; explain isotopes as same-element different-neutron atoms; describe alpha, beta and gamma decay; apply half-life calculations; identify applications of radioactivity in medicine and industry.
wider: Examine how Thomson, Millikan and Rutherford experiments provide consistent independent evidence for the nuclear model (AC9S9H01)
Investigate how radiocarbon and other dating methods established that First Peoples of Australia have been present for more than 60,000 years
Examine medical and industrial applications of radioactivity — cancer diagnosis and treatment, flaw detection in aircraft components (AC9S9H02)
Explore how understanding of mass-energy equivalence connects conservation of energy to nuclear processes
elaborations: comparing the mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons
examining how the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons resulted from experimental evidence
explaining that differences in the number of neutrons in atoms of the same element results in isotopes
describing how different unstable isotopes decay such as radon-222, iodine-131 and cobalt-60
defining half-life and simulating radioactive decay
investigating how radiocarbon dating has been used to establish First Peoples' presence for more than 60,000 years
identifying applications of radioactivity in medicine and industry
discussing how mass and energy are connected at all scales

AC9S9U07.minimum_width: Identify reactants and products in at least two reactions; write at least two balanced symbolic equations; explain why equations must be balanced using conservation of mass; explain mass change in open vs closed systems.
AC9S9U07.typical_width: Identify reactants and products; explain atomic rearrangement using models; write and balance simple symbolic equations; investigate reactions in closed and open systems; relate mass data to conservation of mass; compare information conveyed by molecular models vs balanced equations.
wider: Investigate chemical reactions First Nations Australians use to convert toxic plants into edible food products — examining traditional food processing chemistry
Examine green chemistry principles — minimising waste products, energy use and environmental impact — and predict how they will change industrial chemistry practice
Investigate why most elements are not found in their elemental state and examine processes used to obtain them — connecting equilibrium concepts to real extraction chemistry
elaborations: identifying reactants and products in chemical reactions
using models and representations to show the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions
investigating chemical reactions in closed and open systems and relating data obtained to the law of conservation of mass
writing symbolic equations that are easy to balance and explaining, using the law of conservation of mass, and atoms, the rationale for balancing chemical equations
investigating why most elements are not found in their elemental state
predicting how ideas of green chemistry will affect the environment
